title: Synthetic Health Suite Implementation and SLO Migration Guide
author: Priya Shah
body:
Overview

This runbook describes how Customer Success (CS) and Support teams implement a standardized Synthetic Health Suite for enterprise tenants, and how to migrate existing per-tenant SLOs to a multi-dimensional SLO model used in QBRs. The goal is to compress detection-to-remediation time, improve fidelity of incident escalation for inference regressions, and centralize metrics used in Customer QBRs.

Audience

- Customer Success, Support, and Oncall engineers
- Platform/Monitoring owners (dashboards/alerting)
- Solutions Engineers who implement tenant instrumentation during onboarding

When to use this document

- During enterprise onboarding (week 1–4) to provision synthetic checks
- When customers request production-grade SLOs or ask to migrate from simple latency-only SLOs
- Prior to a QBR where synthetic coverage and SLO changes will be reviewed

Key definitions

- Synthetic Health Suite: a set of automated, scheduled requests that exercise a customer’s production inference path with representative prompts and assertions (latency, correctness, token-cost).
- Multi-dimensional SLO: an SLO composed of multiple metrics (latency, availability/error rate, and quality/regression) with weighted objectives.
- Check: a single synthetic job (e.g., streaming completion for chat route)

High-level rollout summary

1. Capture tenant profile (input distribution, typical sequence length, model variant).
2. Create synthetic checks (happy path, edge-case correctness, high-throughput pressure) and store config in tenant synthetic repo.
3. Wire checks into the Synthetic Runner (scheduled job service) and monitoring pipeline (Prometheus -> Cortex -> Grafana).
4. Define multi-dimensional SLO and thresholds; create dashboard panels and alert rules.
5. Validate for 72 hours, tune thresholds, and add to tenant QBR artifacts.

Tenant profile checklist

- Primary route(s): e.g., /v1/generate-chat, /v1/embeddings
- Representative prompt templates (3–5) and expected tokens-per-response
- Typical concurrency and burst patterns (RPS / minute)
- Accepted latency distribution (p50/p90/p99 targets)
- Quality acceptance criteria (sample eval prompts and golden answers)

Synthetic check types and examples

- Latency check (happy path): ensure p95 < configured target for route.
- Correctness assertion: run evaluation prompts and fuzzy-match responses against golden set (BLEU/ROUGE or embedding-similarity > 0.88).
- Cost sanity check: detect token inflation (per-response tokens suddenly increase > 2x baseline).
- KV-cache smoke: repeated prefix requests should have reduced tail latency by >= 20% vs cold runs.
- Throughput pressure: short burst to validate autoscale & queueing behavior.

Sample synthetic configuration (YAML)

# example synthetic job config for tenant-123
name: tenant-123-chat-happy
route: /v1/generate-chat
schedule: "*/5 * * * *"   # every 5 minutes
payload_templates:
  - id: welcome-1
    prompt: "User: Summarize the following product note in 2 bullets: {text}"
    expected_token_range: "20-80"
assertions:
  - type: latency_p95
    threshold_ms: 600
  - type: embedding_similarity
    prompt_id: welcome-1
    threshold: 0.88
notifications: ["pagerduty:CS-Tenant-Alerts", "slack:#cs-tenant-123"]
owner: se-team@example.com

Implementation steps (detailed)

1) Gather inputs (SE + CS)
   - Owner: Solutions Engineering (SE)
   - Inputs: prompt templates, golden answers, tenant concurrency profile
   - Deliverable: tenant-synthetic.yaml in repo /synthetics/tenant-123.yaml

2) Author synthetic job and test locally
   - Locally run runner: ./synthetic-runner --config tenant-123.yaml --test
   - Validate assertions pass for a minimum of 3 successive runs before scheduling

3) Deploy to Synthetic Runner and enable telemetry pipeline
   - CI step creates job in synthetic scheduler (k8s CronJob or managed scheduler)
   - Metrics emitted: synthetic.latency_ms{tenant,route,check}, synthetic.error_count{...}, synthetic.tokens_per_response{...}

4) Create dashboards and alert rules
   - Grafana panels: p50/p90/p95 latency, error rate (5m), tokens per response, similarity score distribution
   - Prometheus alert examples (rule language):
     - ALERT SyntheticLatencyDegraded
       IF histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(synthetic_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant, route)) > 0.6
       FOR 10m
       LABELS {severity=\"page\"}
       ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Synthetic p95 > 600ms for {{ $labels.tenant }} {{ $labels.route }}\"}

     - ALERT SyntheticQualityRegression
       IF sum(rate(synthetic_similarity_below_threshold[1h])) by (tenant) > 0
       FOR 5m
       LABELS {severity=\"ticket\"}
       ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Quality regression detected for {{ $labels.tenant }}\"}

5) Map alerts to escalation and ownership
   - PagerDuty: Severity=page -> oncall SRE -> if >30min -> Escalate to CS escalation engineer
   - Slack: Severity=ticket -> CS team queue -> SE to triage within 8 business hours

Multi-dimensional SLO model (recommendation)

- SLO composition (example monthly window):
  - Latency objective (weight 0.5): p95 latency <= 600ms for critical routes (target 99.5% success)
  - Availability/objective (weight 0.3): successful responses (HTTP 200 + no model errors) >= 99.9%
  - Quality/regression objective (weight 0.2): similarity to golden responses >= 0.88 for 98% of checks

SLO calculation notes

- Use error budget burn rate dashboards for each tenant. For quality regressions, count the check as failed if similarity < threshold or token inflation > 2x.
- When migrating from a single metric SLO (e.g., p95 latency only): run both SLOs in parallel (shadow mode) for 30 days and compare burn rates before full cutover.

Migration playbook (step-by-step)

1. Baseline (day 0–7): enable synthetic checks and run both old SLO and new multi-dim SLO in shadow.
2. Evaluate (day 8–21): collect burn rate deltas, false positives, and customer impact notes.
3. Tune thresholds (day 22–28): adjust similarity thresholds and latency targets where synthetic coverage is insufficient.
4. Stakeholder sign-off (day 29–33): SE, CS, Oncall, and customer rep sign migration ticket.
5. Cutover (day 34): flip multi-dimensional SLO into production as the authoritative SLO; keep old SLO as read-only archive for 90 days.

Validation and QA checklist

- Synthetic checks run without false positives for 72 hours (<= 1 FP per week acceptable)
- Metrics pipeline latency < 2 minutes end-to-end
- Dashboard panels display tenant-specific metrics and links to sample failing traces
- Playbook entry in customer’s onboarding checklist complete and linked in their QBR artifact bundle

Operator runbook for common failures

- Alert: SyntheticLatencyDegraded
  - Step 1: Confirm scope (tenant and route) and if burst or baseline shift using query: rate(synthetic_requests_total{tenant=\"...\"}[5m])
  - Step 2: Check model variant swaps in last 24h (audit logs: /infra/change-log?tenant=...)
  - Step 3: If KV cache coldness suspected, run warmup: replay 10 recent prefixes to the model and monitor latency; if latency reduces by >= 20% mark incident as KV-cache-related
  - Step 4: If traffic spike, validate autoscaler metrics (gpu_utilization, queue_length); escalate to infra if autoscaler not scaling within 2 minutes

- Alert: SyntheticQualityRegression
  - Step 1: Retrieve last 20 failing synthetic outputs and compute embedding similarity vs golden answers locally
  - Step 2: If regression correlates with a model version rollout, initiate immediate rollback policy per the tenant’s rollout config
  - Step 3: If no rollout correlation, file a quality incident and assign to Applied-ML for triage with example IDs and golden sets

QBR artifacts and reporting

- For each QBR include: synthetic coverage matrix (routes x check types), SLO burn rate trend (90/30/7 days), top 5 failing prompts/examples, remediation actions taken, and action plan for next quarter.
- Slide template: 1) Executive summary, 2) SLO heatmap, 3) Incident highlights (customer impact), 4) Action items and owners

Ownership and contacts

- Synthetic runner & scheduler: eng-platform / owner: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.com)
- Monitoring & alerts: eng-sre / owner: Omar Reyes (omar@redwood.com)
- Applied ML triage (quality): applied-ml / owner: Dr. Nina Kapoor (nina@redwood.com)
- Customer-facing CS lead: assigned per-customer in customer CRM.

Appendix: Useful queries and CLI snippets

- Quick similarity investigation (local python snippet):
  python -c \"from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util; m=SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2'); a=m.encode('golden'); b=m.encode('candidate'); print(util.cos_sim(a,b))\"

- Prometheus query: p95 latency for tenant-123 over last 1h
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(synthetic_latency_bucket{tenant=\"tenant-123\"}[1h])) by (le))

- Create synthetic job via API (curl):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    https://internal-synthetics.redwood/api/v1/jobs \
    -d '{"name":"tenant-123-chat-happy","schedule":"*/5 * * * *","route":"/v1/generate-chat","payload_template_id":"welcome-1"}'

Notes and best practices

- Keep golden answer sets short (5–20 examples) and refresh quarterly as product prompts evolve.
- Avoid including customer PII in synthetic inputs; use pseudonymized data from onboarding export.
- For latency objectives, synthetic runs should mimic real latency distribution (e.g., realistic token-lengths and system prompt context).
